item.title: American citizen among at least 12 people killed in blast at Saudi Arabia airport
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Timour Azhari and Enas Alashray RIYADH, Oct 10 (Reuters) - At least 12 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in an attack on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, as the Iran-backed Houthis escalate a campaign they launched this summer. The ‌dead from the third attack this week on the airport included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, ‌Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, 309 were wounded, officials said. President Donald Trump said Washington was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover ​from the war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, some in critical condition after the attack, which occurred without warning. CONFLICT ESCALATES AFTER YEMEN WAR CEASEFIRE UNRAVELS The two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport this week killed four and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac. The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as it wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group. The Houthis ‌have not claimed responsibility for the attack, but a Saudi-led ⁠military coalition vowed to respond. Trump, asked whether the US planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, told reporters: "We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly." US Secretary of State ⁠Marco Rubio condemned the attacks on the airport, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life". UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also condemned Saturday's strike, reiterating that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international law and must cease immediately. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis have said these killed civilians including women and children. ​Reuters ​could not independently verify those claims. The Saudis entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of ​an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the ‌Yemeni capital Sanaa. The war became a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. A 2022 ceasefire reached by the Saudis and the Houthis unravelled this summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces. EXPLOSION, PEOPLE ON GROUND, AMBULANCES RUSHING The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, but it has made only slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege. On Saturday, all flights were diverted from Riyadh and operations at the airport that serves a city of 8 million people were suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. The head of the ‌Houthi media office posted on X that the group had "shut down Riyadh international airport". The Houthis have ​said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations. The Houthis have warned international ​airlines against operating flights through Saudi airspace, saying it has become a theatre ​of their military operations, with the exception of airspace over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. An eyewitness at the airport reported seeing an ‌explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. ​More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing ​towards the facility. A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport. An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed. The US embassy in Riyadh said it "strongly recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas." Earlier Houthi attacks had ​prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services ‌to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences. Organizers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes ​on Saturday they would go ahead as planned. (Reporting by Timour Azhari in Riyadh; Additional reporting by Steve Holland in Washington; Writing by Enas Alashray, Maya ​Gebeily and Ann Saphir; Editing by Gareth Jones, Joe Bavier, David Gregorio and William Mallard) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/loud-blast-heard-riyadh-airport-141257574.html

item.title: Trump says Ukraine should get a new president as he blames Zelensky for diesel prices
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end his country’s war with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S. “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said. The president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure . He has also sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices. “He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel,” Trump said, before departing for Tennessee where he was set to rally Republican voters. Ukrainian and European officials on Saturday reacted to Trump's diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war efforts. Diesel prices have skyrocketed due to a collision of events , including the difficulty of getting oil out of the Middle East since the start of the Iran war, which has raised the price of all oil products. An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll conducted last month and published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of Iran, and blame him for higher prices. Trump also suggested that if he had been U.S. president in 2022, “that war would have never started. There was no reason that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence.” Zelenskyy has “lost 30% of your country and you’ve had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That’s a war that should have never started. And I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump said. Independent estimates are that about 20% of Ukraine's territory is under Russian control. British defense officials recently estimated that about half a million Russian soldiers have been killed in the war; there are no reliable recent estimates about how many Ukrainians have died. 20 people killed in Russian bombing in Ukraine Saturday Trump's extraordinary intervention came after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian officials said Saturday. Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Saturday. At least 18 people were wounded. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days. Anger in Kyiv at Trump’s deal with Putin “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote Saturday on X. He said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive, and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defenses, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days. Trump announced Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. In Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation. “Trump has once again shown his true face,” said Oleksandr Petrenko, 26. “He didn’t care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he’s interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay.” For Oksana Yakunina, a financial adviser from the central city of Kropyvnytskyi, the announcement “didn’t really come as a surprise.” “Trump has been working with Putin for a long time,” she told The Associated Press. European allies question US-Russia deal Ukraine's European allies also expressed dismay at the deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said Stockholm regretted the agreement, “as energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest,” and noted that the European Union would adopt its most comprehensive sanctions package yet on Monday, with 1,600 listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex. The German government “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions,” spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering.” Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski questioned whether Russia could deliver at all. Citing his embassy’s reports of fuel shortages even in Moscow, and “serious sources” saying Ukraine has damaged about half of Russia’s refining capacity, he asked on X: “So where will the surpluses for export come from?” Trump’s announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine. Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war. Speaking about Friday’s announcement, a senior Ukrainian official told AP that the Ukrainian side was not aware of the deal before the announcement. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorized to discuss the issue publicly, said Saturday the diesel deal announcement was not tied to anything under discussion in Florida. He confirmed the Ukrainian delegation had left Florida and were on their way back to Ukraine. ___ Daly reported from Washington and Morton reported from London. Associated Press journalists Bela Szandelszky in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Collin Binkley in Washington contributed to this report. ___ Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/russian-attacks-kill-7-ukraine-071733676.html

item.title: Philadelphia police officer and partner shot while responding to report of armed man
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A Philadelphia police officer died Saturday after he and his partner were ambushed and shot multiple times while responding to a report of an armed man in the western part of the city. Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner identified the suspect as 35-year-old Eric Lewis, who has a criminal record dating back to 2012, according to Pennsylvania court records reviewed by Fox News Digital. A municipal labor union also identified Lewis as an employee of the Philadelphia Water Department. Krasner outlined a series of charges stemming from the shooting, including attempted murder, attempted homicide of a law enforcement officer, aggravated assault and gun offenses. Prosecutors identified at least 11 potential victims, including the two officers who were shot and nine additional people who were fired upon. Connecticut Police Officers Shot, Suspect Killed After Attempted Arrest Sparks Hectic Chase Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel identified the officer who died as Shane Seiber, a 40-year-old father who spent 10 years on the force. Read On The Fox News App He leaves behind his wife and his two children, a 7-year-old son and a 3-year-old daughter. Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel, pictured here May 8, 2025, gave an update on the officers shot while responding to a call in the western part of the city Oct. 10, 2026. "He fought valiantly, but he lost his life today," Bethel said at a morning news conference. "His wife was able to be by his side before he passed, as well as his family." Lewis was found guilty of theft and receiving stolen property in 2012 and gun-related offenses and simple assault in 2013, receiving probation in both cases, according to court records. In 2018, Lewis pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct involving fighting and was again sentenced to probation. Court records also show Lewis was cited for three traffic violations in 2024, including driving without headlights, failing to provide proof of insurance and windshield-related violations. District Council 33, a labor union representing Philadelphia municipal workers, identified Lewis as one of its members and an employee of the Philadelphia Water Department in a Facebook statement addressing the shooting. The union condemned the violence, expressed condolences to Seiber's family and wished the surviving officer a full recovery. District Council 33 also said it would cooperate with authorities as the case proceeds. During a news conference, Mayor Cherelle Parker said Seiber "paid the ultimate price while sacrificing his own life to protect and serve our city." Parker also announced plans to seek legislation expanding Pennsylvania's involuntary commitment laws to cover substance use disorders and other mental or behavioral health conditions. She said she would work with Gov. Josh Shapiro, the state legislature and Attorney General Dave Sunday on the proposal. The Philadelphia police officers were shot a total of 15 times, according to officials. Krasner also declined to discuss the suspect's motive, citing the ongoing investigation and sensitivity toward the victims' families. The mayor also referenced the deaths of nine people in Erie, Pennsylvania, saying the tragedy underscored the need to revisit existing laws. Parker acknowledged that investigators had not determined whether mental health or substance use played a role in the Erie deaths. Parker separately ordered city flags to remain at half-staff until sunset on the day of Seiber's interment. Gov. Shapiro said in a social media post that he and his wife were praying for Seiber's loved ones and the Philadelphia Police Department. He also ordered all U.S. and state flags to be flown at half-staff. Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., also mourned Seiber's death, offering prayers for his family, the Philadelphia Police Department and the wounded officer. McCormick said Philadelphia had lost a hero whose sacrifice would not be forgotten. The two Philadelphia police officers who were shot were taken to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center. Rep. Mike Kelly, R-Pa., separately offered prayers for the Erie community and the families affected by Friday night's tragedy. The other officer, a 33-year-old father of five children, was shot 12 times and was initially in critical condition. After going into surgery, Bethel said, he is now in stable condition but is "not out of the woods yet." Just after 12:20 a.m., the officers responded to a report of a man with a gun on a porch, Bethel said. About 30 minutes later, the officers arrived at the address and came under "significant gunfire" once they were on the porch. Shortly after shots were fired, Bethel said, additional officers and a SWAT team found the original responding officers on the porch with gunshot wounds. After running away, the suspect fired at two additional officers, Bethel said. Krasner outlined nine additional counts of attempted murder and attempted homicide of a law enforcement officer involving the nine other people who were fired upon. A SWAT team was able to locate the suspect in a tree and take him into custody. Krasner said Lewis remained in custody without serious injuries and was expected to appear for a preliminary arraignment and bail hearing. item.title: Mystery at Russian plague lab as WHO struggles to explain young worker's death
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
GENEVA (AP) — The World Health Organization said Saturday it still doesn’t know what caused the death of a young worker at a lab in Russia that focuses on plague and other illnesses. The U.N. health agency has cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. Pneumonic plague spreads from person to person, causing a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time. WHO, in its first full Disease Outbreak News since the case emerged earlier this month, called for a continued investigation. Russian health officials, it said, had conducted more than 5,500 tests and found no evidence of any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms. “Additional clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information, including confirmation of the diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker, is required to improve confidence in the assessment,” WHO said. WHO continued to refer to “a purported second case” that, in emailed explanations to The Associated Press, it previously attributed to two tabloid news outlets in Britain and Serbia that cited unspecified reports in Russia. Russia has denied any such second case. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/mystery-surrounds-young-workers-death-201307325.html

item.title: Pentagon raises official toll of troops who died during war with Iran to 21
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Pentagon acknowledged late Friday that the number of troops who have died in the Middle East during its operations against Iran is higher than previously reported, and updated the official count to include two more noncombat deaths. The Washington Post exclusively reported last month, based on information from six U.S. officials, that the numbers of service members lost was greater than what the Pentagon was reporting in its official, public database, known as the Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the time called that reporting "a complete lie" in a social media post. However, late Friday, the Pentagon raised the figure publicly reported in DCAS to include additional deaths. As of Friday, the total troop deaths the administration is connecting to operations against Iran and officially reporting in DCAS stands at 21. That figure includes two additional noncombat deaths: Maj. Sorffly Davius, 46, an Army National Guard member who died in Kuwait on March 6, and an unidentified Navy suicide that occurred in September, according to a U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to provide additional context on the troop deaths. In addition, 865 service members have been wounded, according to updated data in DCAS. The military also acknowledged one additional soldier's training accident death that it said was not tied to ongoing operations against Iran. Sgt. Devin A. Seibel, 26, died during a training accident in Iraq in May. His death is now recorded in DCAS under Operation Inherent Resolve, the military's decade-long named operation against the Islamic State. That service member's death brings the total number of troops who have died in the Middle East since Feb. 28, the date that operations against Iran began, to 22. On Friday, two of the top Democratic members of the House Armed Services Committee said they were glad the Pentagon had made a "public correction" to the overall losses in the war. "There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude," the committee's top Democrat, Rep. Adam Smith (Washington) and Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (Pennsylvania), the top Democrat on the military personnel subcommittee, said in a statement, calling the fact that Congress had to get involved to have the Pentagon correct its numbers "an embarrassment" for the military. In a statement to The Post, the Pentagon did not acknowledge the changed numbers but instead said it is making further revisions to how DCAS reports casualties, including a new category of "pending adjudication" as it works through casualty reporting. The new adjudication category was first reported by Defense Scoop. The Pentagon "continues to maintain a steadfast commitment to the transparent, accurate accounting of all Service member casualties," it said in a statement. It has been difficult for the public and lawmakers overseeing the Pentagon to get a clear picture of how many troops have been injured or killed during the conflict in part because the Trump administration changed mid-conflict the way it was publicly accounting for troop deaths, something critics have charged is a way for President Donald Trump to hide the true cost to military personnel. In previous conflicts those injuries or deaths - whether caused by hostile action or nonhostile causes, such as accidents or suicides - have been captured by named conflict in DCAS. In part, what has confounded DCAS data in this conflict is that earlier this year Trump declared that Operation Epic Fury had ended, even though the U.S. and Iran were still exchanging fire. In response the Pentagon created a new category of injured and killed that was not tied to Epic Fury, instead those numbers would be tallied under overseas contingency operations. item.title: Man kills 8 people, including children and relatives, in Pennsylvania home, police say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A man killed eight people including a pregnant woman, children and other relatives at his home in Erie, Pennsylvania, before taking his own life as well, authorities said Saturday. Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said the 45-year-old man was related to seven of the victims in the previous day's shooting, while the eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman. Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door shortly before 5 p.m. Friday, he said. The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside. Police arrived to find the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of a 5-year-old boy; a 1-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor. “Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference. “But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole.” Lorah declined to discuss motive but said investigators would talk to other relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home. “They knew something was going on at that house,” he said. “We have to figure out what that is.” Lorah said officers arrived within minutes of receiving an alert via ShotSpotter , a controversial gunshot detection system that relies on artificial intelligence and a network of microphones to identify gunshots. No additional shots were fired after that. “Sounds that may have been mistaken for gunfire came from flashbang devices — chemical munitions — used by SWAT officers,” he said. Gov. Josh Shapiro said he offered his administration's “full support” to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin, who spoke directly to the victims' families during the news conference. “I am so deeply sorry. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier,” she said. “But you do need to know that our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.” District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz urged the public to refrain from speculation as the investigation continues. “Please do not allow rumors, speculation or unverified information to add to the pain that these families are already experiencing,” she said. Erie is about 120 miles (190 kilometers) north of Pittsburgh. Speaking at a campaign rally outside Philadelphia, Shapiro mentioned both the Erie killings and the shooting of two Philadelphia police officers early Saturday. “Today has been a dark day across this commonwealth,” he said. ____ This story corrects that the total number of people found dead — nine — includes the suspected shooter. ____ Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Jacqueline GaNun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues. item.title: Rare 'sting jet' unleashes 117 mph winds as Hurricane Isaias pummels Florida
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias was moving northeast through central Alabama near Birmingham on Saturday after roaring ashore as a Category 2 hurricane late Friday evening near Destin, Florida, with winds of about 105 mph, causing at least four deaths. Trees and power lines were down in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle, creating dangerous conditions and forcing road closures late Friday, officials said. Power outages are in the hundreds of thousands of homes and businesses across much of Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and western Georgia. At least four people have been reported killed in the storm, two each in Alabama and Florida, authorities said Saturday. The storm broke a two-year drought of U.S. hurricane landfalls, with the most recent being Hurricane Milton in October 2024, two years to the day before Isaias made landfall. The center of Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias was moving north over Alabama on Saturday and is expected to reach the Tennessee Valley later in the day and into Sunday, when it will make a northeastward turn. As of 5 p.m. ET Saturday, the center of Isaias was about 5 miles west of Birmingham, Alabama, moving northeast at 15 mph, according to the National Weather Service . The storm is forecast to continue inland and weaken further. 95% of affected customers should have power restored by Monday, FPL says 09:09 PM ET, October 10 2026, Lisa Nellessen Savage Florida Power and Light says it expects to have 95% of affected customers who can "safely accept power" to be restored by end of day Monday, Oct. 12. Many of those customers are expected to have a power back sooner, FPL said it a statement Saturday night. As of 7:30 p.m. local time, 122,830 Escambia County customers were still without power, as well as 78,590 customers in Santa Rosa County and 44,740 customers in Okaloosa County. Curfew in effect for Santa Rosa County 08:21 PM ET, October 10 2026, Tom McLaughlin Santa Rosa County Sheriff Bob Johnson announced that a countywide curfew will be in effect from dusk until dawn until the local state of emergency declared ahead of the arrival of Hurricane Isaias has been lifted. Johnson said the curfew was being implemented not only as a precaution against looting, but also because approximately 80% of traffic lights in the county had been disabled during the storm. Pensacola airport to reopen Sunday 08:14 PM ET, October 10 2026, Jim Little The Pensacola International Airport terminal will fully open for regularly scheduled commercial service Sunday, Oct. 11. Passengers are advised to check with individual airlines for the most up-to-date flight info. The airport had been closed indefinitely as officials assessed the damage from Isaias, but the runway is open for noncommercial flights. Water services restored to Pensacola Beach 08:10 PM ET, October 10 2026 Emerald Coast Utilities Authority announced that it restored water and sewer services to Pensacola Beach Saturday evening. Residents remain under a systemwide precautionary boil water notice, which will remain in effect until further notice. School officials assess damage in Florida 05:38 PM ET, October 10 2026 Public schools in Escambia and Santa Rosa counties in Florida will be closed Monday, Oct. 12, as the districts continue to assess damage from Hurricane Isaias. Students were scheduled to be off for the Columbus Day holiday even before the storm, but teachers were planned to be on camps for planning and development activities. In a statement Superintendent Karen Barber said, "We district to survey damages and make any necessary plans and adjustments." Plans for Tuesday, Oct. 13, and beyond will depend on information received about the status of area schools. 'Sting jet' phenomenon caused tornado-like wind gusts up to 117 mph 04:55 PM ET, October 10 2026, Benjamin Johnson Although the National Weather Service has not confirmed any tornadoes amid the damage left by Hurricane Isaias, meteorologists say a "rare and unusual" phenomenon called a "sting jet" caused tornado-like wind gusts throughout the west side of the hurricane. A sting jet, according to NWS meteorologists, occurred when drier air ran into the sharp western edge of Isaias, causing rapidly sinking evaporated cool air to rush downwards from the top of the storm to the surface of Earth. That jetting air caused enhanced wind gusts, such as the 117 mph gust recorded on Santa Rosa Island and the 114 mph gust recorded in Milton at NAS Whiting Field. Those sting jets produce tornado-like winds and cause significant wind damage. Isaias' winds rivaled Ivan's in Florida counties 03:58 PM ET, October 10 2026, Brandon Girod The National Weather Service's preliminary high wind report for Hurricane Isaias shows strong gusts throughout Escambia and Santa Rosa counties in Florida. The strongest gusts were recorded in Santa Rosa County. A 117-mph gust was recorded at 7:30 p.m. at Oriole Beach, a 116-mph gust was reported near the Santa Rosa Sound at 7:45 p.m. and NAS Whiting Field reported a 114-mph gust at 8:37 p.m. The strongest gust reported in Escambia was 105 mph in Ferry Pass at 6:29 p.m. Pensacola City Hall reported a 102-mph gust at the same time. The strongest gust recorded in Escambia County during Hurricane Ivan was 107 mph at the Pensacola Naval Air Station. Harold recorded the strongest gust in Santa Rosa County at 90 mph. A 119 mph gust was reported in Mary Esther, and a whopping 145-mph gust was unofficially recorded by a sailboat anchored in Wolf Bay in Baldwin County, Alabama, according to the National Weather Service. US authorizes emergency exchange of crude oil from Strategic Petroleum Reserve for Isaias disruptions 03:49 PM ET, October 10 2026, Doyle Rice The US Energy Department said Saturday that it had authorized an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address supply disruptions due to Hurricane Isaias. “With this emergency exchange, the Energy Department is acting swiftly to help maintain refinery operations, limit disruptions to fuel supplies, and ensure American families and businesses continue to have access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy,” U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said in a statement. – Reuters Power restoration hampered by debris, DeSantis says 03:23 PM ET, October 10 2026, Jeanine Santucci Crews have been out since before daylight clearing roads of downed trees, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in an afternoon update Saturday. Linemen are also working to restore power to the hundreds of thousands of Floridians in the dark, he said. Crews have needed to get debris out of the way before they can reconnect power, DeSantis said. "There's just a lot of trees that interfere," he said. There are more than 426,000 homes and businesses without power as of 3 p.m. ET. Wind shear knocked down Isaias' power before landfall 03:18 PM ET, October 10 2026, Doyle Rice and Kimberly Miller Meteorologists said the forecasts for the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season were generally on target, although a nail-biter at the end as National Hurricane Center experts grappled with timing on when wind shear would ultimately start to tear down the storm. It had just a six-hour window that could make the difference between a Category 2 and Category 3 hurricane reaching the coast. The promised storm-toppling wind shear finally appeared in the end, hammering down Hurricane Isaias' winds from a Category 3 to a 105-mph Category 2 storm at landfall, but with a sweep of storm surge already locked in as the widening cyclone reached the coast. "There are a lot of moving parts," said Michael Fischer, an assistant professor in the University of Miami's Department of Atmospheric Sciences at the Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric and Earth Science. "The sea-surface temperatures are really warm and raise the ceiling on how strong a storm can get and those warm temperatures can offset the harmful effects of shear." At least 4 dead in Isaias aftermath 02:12 PM ET, October 10 2026, Jeanine Santucci Authorities on Saturday have updated the death toll from Hurricane Isaias to at least four people, two each in Alabma and Florida. Alabama Two were killed in Alabama, Gov. Kay Ivey said in a statement Saturday at about noon ET. "I am praying for their loved ones this morning," she said. Ivey did not give further details on the fatalities. One of the deaths happened in Birmingham early Saturday morning when a tree fell on a home, Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker previously told USA TODAY. Florida Two people have also died in Escambia County, Florida, Sgt. Melony Peterson with the the sheriff's office confirmed. The first happened late Friday night after a large tree fell on a home, pinning the victim underneath. On Saturday, the sheriff's office responded to a home where a person was found deceased inside a closed garage where a generator was running. Andy Hazelton, a meteorologist and hurricane researcher at the University of Miami, said on X Saturday that it's "probably a low probability chance at this point, but it might be worth watching the northwest Caribbean for development in about a week." He added that models indicate a tropical wave may interact with the end of a front and also find itself in an upper-air pattern favorable for storms. "Right now, I think it's most likely that this just gets shoved into Central America without doing much, but it'll be worth watching if the signal increases over time. "Right now about 10-20% of DeepMind members are developing something," he said. (DeepMind is Google's AI research powerhouse, known for advanced weather-forecasting models.) Trapped in the eye of the storm 01:35 PM ET, October 10 2026, Dinah Voyles Pulver A crew on an Air Force Reserve Hurricane Hunter flying into the center of the hurricane on Friday, Oct. 9, spotted a white bird trapped in the calm center. The bird, an egret, flew across the pilot's view at a lower altitude from the plane, the crew reported in its message with flight data to the National Hurricane Center. Matt Devitt, a Florida meteorologist, also reported in an X post that birds were seen inside the eye of Isaias through Doppler radar. It's not uncommon for birds to be trapped in the calm center of the storm, commonly called the "eye." Experts say Birds sometimes try to fly around a storm and get diverted, according to experts, or they get caught up in an outer band and ride with it until they reach land or drop into the ocean. In August 2023 Hurricane Idalia brought brought a flamboyance of flamingos to the U.S. East Coast . Flamingoes were eventually seen as far north as Cape Cod and Wisconsin. Our thoughts are with the communities facing Hurricane Isaias and the first responders helping them. This footage offers a view from the Air Force Reserve Hurricane Hunters’ mission into the storm, where crews collected weather data to support National Hurricane Center… pic.twitter.com/THvvpzAAmM — Hurricane Hunters (@53rdWRS) October 10, 2026 Milton and Isaias: Two hurricanes, two years apart 01:27 PM ET, October 10 2026, Doyle Rice WeatherNation calls it tropical deja-vu: Two hurricanes, almost exactly two years apart. Both Hurricane Milton (2024) and Hurricane Isaias (2026) made landfall on October 9th on the Gulf side of Florida. In addition, their landfalls were only also only an hour apart from each other, WeatherNation said in a post on X. Milton hit at 8:30 p.m. EDT, while Isaias hit at 8:30 p.m. CDT. Isaias was the first hurricane to hit the United States since Milton, which hit Siesta Key, Florida, as a Category 3 storm with winds of 120 mph. Milton spawned dozens of tornadoes and led to major wind, flooding, and surge damage across Florida. See photos: Floridians survey the damage from Isaias 12:52 PM ET, October 10 2026, Jeanine Santucci Photos from around the Florida Panhandle show extensive damage on Saturday morning. In Gulf Breeze, Florida, a truck is seen overturned in standing water in a parking lot. The front panel of a gas pump at a gas station was torn off. Trees were overturned onto houses and roadways. A roadway in Navarre, Florida, was hardly visible beneath fallen branches. Even though the center of the hurricane hit in Destin, Florida, roughly 45-50 miles east of Pensacola, the winds were still strong enough in Pensacola to cause damages. AccuWeather correspondent Ali Reid documented extensive destruction from Isaias across Pensacola from trees down and multiple businesses with damage, according to a report from AccuWeather. As of 11 a.m. ET, the center of Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias was located about 50 miles south of Birmingham, Alabama. It packed sustained winds of 35 mph and was moving to the north-northwest at 10 mph. "Maximum sustained winds are near 35 mph with higher gusts, especially in areas of elevated terrain. The NASCAR Cup Series Bank of America 400 is now scheduled for Sunday at 3 p.m. ET, with the O'Reilly race slated to run after that, weather permitting. Racing on Sunday may be problematic as the National Weather Service is predicting an 80% chance of rain in Charlotte. Map shows where the heaviest rain is expected today 11:00 AM ET, October 10 2026, Doyle Rice Heavy rain from the remnants of Hurricane Isaias will plague much of the southeastern U.S. over the weekend, forecasters from NOAA's Weather Prediction Center said Saturday. A map from the WPC (below) shows where excessive rainfall is most likely Saturday. The WPC said that the heaviest rains are likely into the upslope regions of the southern Appalachians from northeast Georgia into the upstate of South Carolina and western North Carolina. "Strong upslope flow will support heavy precipitation totals in the 3-5 inch range across these areas, with maximum totals in the 6-10 inch range across far western North Carolina into the Upstate of South Carolina," the WPC said in an online forecast. The greatest threats Saturday for tornadoes are in southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, southwestern Georgia and southern South Carolina, according to AccuWeather. On Sunday, the tornado risk will shift to eastern North Carolina, eastern South Carolina and southeastern Virginia. Isaias leaves more than 800,000 without power 10:51 AM ET, October 10 2026, Mike Snider More than 800,000 Americans along the Gulf Coast are without power Saturday after the high winds and heavy rains brought by Hurricane Isaias . Hundreds of thousands of outages have been reported across much of Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and western Georgia, according to USA TODAY's outage tracker . Crews have been making progress, with power restored to nearly 100,000 homes and businesses by 10:30 a.m. ET – about 900,000 were without power just an hour earlier, according to the outage tracker. The storm, which made landfall Friday night in Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 hurricane, brought destructive winds , torrential rain and dangerous storm surge, AccuWeather said. Isaias has since weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, but the potential for additional outages remains as the storm is expected to continue unleashing winds of 40 to 60 mph and rain of 4-8 inches as it moves north into South Carolina and North Carolina, according to AccuWeather. Outages along the Gulf Coast and farther inland, according to USA TODAY's outage tracker, which uses utility companies outage maps: Alabama – 283,869 Florida – 460,002 Georgia – 116,230 North Carolina – 6,220 Tennessee – 5,922 South Carolina – 2,728 1 dead in Birmingham, Alabama 10:16 AM ET, October 10 2026, Jeanine Santucci One person is dead in Birmingham, Alabama, after a tree fell on a home, Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told USA TODAY. The person was killed when a tree fell on a home early Saturday morning as Isaias moved through the state, Coker said. The tree fell in the Huffman area of Birmingham, the emergency management agency said in a statement. "Across Jefferson County, we have received multiple reports of trees damaging homes. At this time, we are not aware of any additional storm-related injuries," the statement said. The death brings the reported toll from Isaias to two, with another death confirmed in Escambia County, Florida. The National Weather Service in Mobile, Alabama, said that some of the strongest wind gusts occurred "surprisingly far" to the west of the storm's center. The top measured gusts included a 117 mph gust on Santa Rosa Island and a 114 mph gust at Whiting Field near Milton. "We have received reports of SIGNIFICANT wind damage stretching all the way from Pensacola northward into Conecuh and Wilcox Counties in Alabama," the weather service wrote. Tropical Storm Rachel takes aim on Southern California 08:49 AM ET, October 10 2026, Doyle Rice Just as folks in the southeastern U.S. are cleaning up and coping with the aftereffects of Hurricane Isaias, Californians are dealing with a rare visit from a tropical storm. Moisture from Tropical Storm Rachel is forecast to bring heavy rain, flash flooding, and high winds to Southern California, the Southwest, and Great Basin late Saturday into Sunday, NOAA's Weather Prediction Center (WPC) said in an online forecast. Rachel, still over the eastern Pacific, is forecast to come ashore in Mexico, then cross the California state line as a tropical storm, depression or tropical wind and rainstorm later this weekend, AccuWeather said. There is a risk of life-threatening flash flooding across the desert canyons and arroyos of the southwestern United States. To the north, a separate storm will move into the Northwest and northern Rockies with snow forecast for the northern Rockies, the WPC said. "The heaviest snow is expected for higher mountain elevations with totals of 6-12 inches, locally higher, possible. Some snow is also expected for lower valley elevations as well as the immediate High Plains east of the Rockies, with some lighter accumulations expected. The snow should taper off later Sunday into Monday." The only official tropical storm landfall in Southern California was in 1939. Multiple storms have come close to making landfall since then with Hilary from 2023 being the most recent, AccuWeather said. Rain from a separate system, now Hurricane Simon, may reach New Mexico and the Great Plains early next week, according to AccuWeather. Isaias joins list of October hurricanes to hit Florida 08:48 AM ET, October 10 2026, Doyle Rice Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, at 8:30 p.m. CDT Friday as a powerful Category 2 hurricane, hammering the western Florida Panhandle with destructive winds, torrential rain and dangerous storm surge, AccuWeather said. Isaias is the fourth October Florida landfalling hurricane since 2000, according to Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach, writing on X. "The other three were: Wilma (2005), Michael (2018) and Milton (2024)." item.title: Hurricane victim's husband says tree crashed through Florida home and pinned his wife
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
( NewsNation ) — Joey Williams, the husband of a woman who died in Florida as Hurricane Isaias battered Gulf Coast states, is remembering his wife as an "ultra-nice badass person" whom everyone loved. Jenn Biggs Williams, 57, worked in human resources. She and Joey were married for a decade. She is the first known fatality of Hurricane Isaias, which struck the Gulf Coast over the weekend. A person in Birmingham, Alabama, also died in connection with the storm, the Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency director confirmed. 4 dead from storm as Isaias brings threat of floods across the Southeast Williams said that as the storm moved through, the couple went outside to take pictures of the sky and some of the damage it had caused. When they went back inside, a tree fell through the roof and into the living room, trapping both of them beneath it. "I was able to squeeze out. My wife didn't make it," Williams told NewsNation. "The tree just fell on her and it was ... we like to think it was pretty instant, you know? I mean, just gone. Gone." Williams said he was able to crawl out and began calling for his wife. "I couldn't ... there's nothing, you know?" he said. He got a neighbor to help as the storm continued to produce winds of up to 100 mph. Jenn Biggs Williams "I'm like, 'My wife's trapped under the tree. Please, please,'" he said. "And, I mean, there's nothing we can do." They called emergency services, but Williams said responders told him their ability to help was limited as the storm intensified. By the time crews arrived and were able to cut up the tree and pull her out, it was too late. The coroner's office was called to the scene. Isaias disrupts holiday weekend travel "They let me say bye to her," he said. "I watched the love of my life for 10 years go into the back of a coroner's van and head down that road. That's the hardest thing I ever swallowed in my life." Williams said his wife was beloved. "Everybody loved her, right? Even her co-workers," he said. "She was the ultra-nice badass person." "I just want to hear her voice," he continued. "I've called her phone five times just to tell her ... she was my world." Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved.
